title: Practice: spot a misleading training score

messages.content: Let me practise choosing a model from learning curves, without being told which concept to use.

content.text: Try this on your own. Write down your reasoning as you go.

arguments.statement: Three checkpoints have (training error, validation error): A = (0.25, 0.28), B = (0.10, 0.16), C = (0.01, 0.30). You must choose one checkpoint, then report its performance. Which checkpoint do you choose, what evidence supports that choice, and what data should you use for the final report?
arguments.modelSolution: Choose B because it has the lowest validation error among the candidates. C's better training fit does not imply better performance on held-out examples; its validation error is higher. After selecting B, evaluate it on a separate untouched test set and report that result with the evaluation conditions.

content.text: Problem posed. The learner's thinking and answer will follow.

messages.content:
Your thinking:
C looks impressive only on the examples used for training. B has the best validation result. I should avoid presenting the score that I repeatedly used to choose the model as an independent final check.

messages.content: I choose B using validation error, and evaluate it on a separate test set. C's lower training error alone is not evidence that it will generalise better.

arguments.verdict: Solved independently. You used validation for selection, recognised the training/validation gap, and kept a separate test evaluation.
